newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian tax arrears seen as barrier to IMF loans.
newsitem.headline: Russian tax arrears seen as barrier to IMF loans.

text.p: Low Russian tax revenues are still a major barrier to big loans from the International Monetary Fund, a source familiar with talks between Russia and the IMF said on Thursday.

But the IMF might decide in mid-May to release some of the hundreds of millions of dollars it has withheld this year, as a gesture of support to the new reformist cabinet, said the source, who requested anonymity.
No one was available to comment at the IMF office in Moscow.
"The tax position continues to be a major problem... the tax side is really pretty awful," the source said.

Russia has come under criticism for a highly inefficient tax collection system which allows widespread evasion, meaning the government is constantly short of revenue. But President Boris Yeltsin won a favourable reaction from the West by installing reformers in a cabinet reshuffle last month.
The IMF has already delayed paying several tranches of its $10 billion three-year loan to Russia and a mission will visit Moscow from April 23 to 25 for talks on the economy.
Payments are linked to Russia meeting monthly targets on the budget deficit, net currency reserves, revenues and net domestic assets -- the monetary base less net reserves.

But tax collection in the first quarter of this year was only 58 percent of budgeted levels, prompting the government to draw up plans to seek authority from parliament to sequester, or cut, spending. The head of the State Tax Service has resigned.
The collapse of tax revenues since last year has worried the IMF, which fears cash shortages could undermine fiscal policy and stifle Russia's nascent economic recovery.
The government has already slashed spending to meet targets for the budget deficit. But this has dampened demand and aggravated the problem of unpaid wages and pensions.
Further sequestration must be approved by the State Duma lower house of parliament, which is dominated by communists.

Alexander Shokhin, a former economy minister who is now first deputy speaker of the Duma, said on Thursday that deputies might fight efforts to cut spending or suggest that Russia print money to pay for services threatened by cuts.
"One cannot rule out that, in the course of that discussion, people will think about proposing a vote of no confidence in the government," he told a news conference.
Ministers say Russia does not necessarily need the IMF money now, because it can fund the budget deficit from the government securities market.
But the IMF's readiness to pay or not to pay the loan is an important signal to foreign investors.
In February the IMF released two tranches of about $325 million each held up from the end of last year. But it has not paid any money for this year.
However, the fund and Russia are close to agreement on the 1997 programme, which may be ready for approval by the IMF board when it meets around May 16.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, in Moscow last week for talks on the 1997 programme, said he was ready to recommend that the fund should approve the plan.
But he said the government must first submit a new tax code to parliament before the IMF paid out. The government has said it plans to submit the final version of the code this month.
A 1997 programme will in principle allow the fund to disburse money already due this year, but it will want to see a major improvement in tax collection first.
But the source said the mission could recommend that the fund release one of this year's delayed tranches, even if tax revenues were underperforming, provided there was progress on the other targets.
"If they go to the board with the 1997 programme, it will be hard not to release some of the 1996 money," the source said.
But the mission could expect to meet strong opposition from officials at IMF headquarters in Washington, especially the fiscal affairs department, to such a soft approach, he said.
